HSCT engines will have much higher jet exhaust speeds compared to today's subsonic airliners.
Jet noise, caused by the turbulent mixing of high-speed exhaust with surrounding air, poses a significant challenge for HSCT engine designers.
HSCT engines use advanced mixer-ejector nozzles to entrain and mix large quantities of ambient air with the jet streams, reducing jet noise to airport noise certification levels.
As the HSCT gains speed and climbs, poor ejector inlet recovery and ejector ram drag contribute to poor thrust, making it advantageous to turn off the ejector.
Turning off the ejector prematurely can cause unacceptable noise levels to propagate to the ground, even when the aircraft is many miles from the airport.
The optimization method employs a variation of the classic energy state approximation technique to dynamically choose the best altitude-velocity path and throttle setting history.
The noise metrics used in the calculations are based on recommendations from researchers at NASA Langley, who have correlated flyover noise annoyance levels with various noise measurements.
HSCT climb noise is characterized by relatively low levels, long durations, and low-frequency spectra, unlike airport noise.
Analysis of the optimizer results has shown significant reductions in noise propagation to the ground can be achieved with only small penalties in HSCT range or fuel performance.
The optimizer is programmed into NASA's existing aircraft and noise analysis codes to balance the tradeoffs between rapid high-altitude climb and quieter low-throttle settings.
The aircraft trajectory, throttle setting, and ejector setting are varied subject to practical aircraft constraints to minimize noise propagation to the ground.

High aircraft altitudes are desirable to minimize noise propagation, but the HSCT may either climb quickly to high altitudes using a high, noisy throttle setting or climb more slowly at a lower, quieter throttle setting.
Throttling operations are performed in the subsonic portion of the climb path where thrust is plentiful, minimizing penalties in HSCT range or fuel performance.
The optimization method aims to determine the optimal timing for turning off the ejector nozzles to balance noise reduction and thrust performance.
The proposed U.S. High Speed Civil Transport (HSCT) will revolutionize commercial air travel by providing economical supersonic passenger service worldwide.
